symbioteFindings: info signature-changed src/languages.ts#Syntax: Syntax changed its signature compatibly; existing users keep working (20 users, 19 untouched)

findings.text: Off-by-one in `rustCharEnd` for simple escapes. `j` points at the backslash, so `\n'` needs `j += 2`, but the code does `j += 3`. That lands one past the closing `'`, so `'\n'`, `'\''`, `'\\'`, `'\0'` and `'\"'` are all rejected and read as lifetimes, even though the goal explicitly lists them as character literals. With `'\"'` (or `b'\"'`) the scanner moves on to the `"` inside and opens a multi-line Rust string. Example: `let q = '\"';` / `// c` / `let s = "x";` gives line 2 as code. After that, comment/code state stays flipped at every later `"` until the next stray quote. The `\u{…}` (line 53) and `\x..` (line 55) branches are correct.

The test 'tells character literals from lifetimes and labels' claims to check `'\''` and `'\\'`, but those lines have no quote, comment opener or trailing comment after the literal. They count as 3 code lines whether or not the literal is recognised, so the test passes despite the bug above. A case like `let q = '\"';` followed by a `// c` line, or `'\'' // c` followed by a comment line, would catch it.

Line 1 starting with `#!` skips the reader, as if it were a shebang. In Rust, `#![…]` on line 1 is an inner attribute, not a shebang, and it is common there. Any comment or string it opens is lost. Examples: `#![allow(x)] /* note` followed by `still comment */`, or `#![doc = r#"` spanning lines; the following lines are miscounted (the comment line becomes code, string lines can become comments). For Rust, only treat it as a shebang when it isn't `#![`.

blind.summary: Swift and Lua match the goal, and so do Rust's comments, strings, raw and byte strings, `\u{…}`/`\x..` escapes and lifetimes. One major bug remains: Rust's simple-escape character literals (`'\n'`, `'\''`, `'\\'`, `'\"'`) are never recognised because of an off-by-one in `rustCharEnd`. With `'\"'` this opens a string that never closes, so every line after it is miscounted. The tests that claim to cover these literals pass anyway, so they don't catch it. Line 1 of a Rust file that starts with `#!` is also skipped as if it were a shebang, so a comment or string opened there is lost.
